Abstract
Materials discovery relies on high-throughput, high-ﬁdelity simulation techniques
such as Density Functional Theory (DFT), which require years of training, exten-
sive parameter ﬁne-tuning and systematic error handling.
To address these chal-
lenges, we introduce the DFT-based Research Engine for Agentic Materials Screen-
ing (DREAMS), a hierarchical, multi-agent framework for DFT simulation that com-
bines a central Large Language Model (LLM) planner agent with domain-speciﬁc LLM
agents for atomistic structure generation, systematic DFT convergence testing, High-
Performance Computing (HPC) scheduling, and error handling. In addition, a shared

with Bayesian ensemble sampling, conﬁrming the Face Centered Cubic (FCC)-site
preference at the Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) DFT level. In conclu-
sion, DREAMS approaches L3-level automation - autonomous exploration of a deﬁned
design space - and signiﬁcantly reduces the reliance on human expertise and inter-
vention, offering a scalable path toward democratized, high-throughput, high-ﬁdelity
computational materials discovery.
Introduction
Materials discovery is a complex, multidimensional challenge that requires signiﬁcant
time, expertise, training, and computational resources. Traditional trial-and-error experi-
ments are resource-intensive and inherently limited in throughput, exploring only a small
fraction of candidates.1 In contrast, computational screening methods—ranging from physics-
based simulations to data-driven methods—offer a powerful alternative to efﬁciently screen-
ing large materials libraries. In this context, physics-based simulations provide fundamen-
tal insights into materials behavior through computational modeling. Density Functional
Theory (DFT) has become the workhorse of computational materials science, enabling
accurate predictions of electronic, structural, and thermodynamic properties at afford-
able computational cost.2 DFT-based computational screening has successfully identiﬁed
promising candidates for energy materials, catalysts, and structural applications.3,4 How-
ever, setting up a DFT-based high-ﬁdelity, high-throughput workﬂow typically requires sub-

introduces cognitive biases that limit the exploration of the design space.6 To address
these limitations, there is growing interest in autonomous materials screening systems
that can minimize the need for human intervention.6 In analogy to self-driving cars and
automated chemical design,7,8 we deﬁne six different levels of automation in computa-
tional materials discovery as shown in Table 1.

Current automation efforts in materials science focus primarily on developing computa-
tional pipelines, a pre-deﬁned execution of speciﬁc tasks. These pipelines are commonly
constructed and executed with workﬂow management systems (WfMS).9–15 The WfMSs
enable the rapid prototyping and up-scaling of reproducible computational workﬂows, still
they are typically hard-coded for speciﬁc tasks, limiting them to level 1 automation. The
predeﬁned nature of their workﬂows means they cannot effectively handle unexpected
errors, without extensive prior preparation or adaptation to screen for novel material prop-
erties.
Large language model (LLM) agents provide a potential solution to this challenge, as
LLM agents combine the reasoning capabilities of LLMs with specialized tools to perform
complex domain-speciﬁc tasks.16 With their ability to reason about problems and dynam-
ically respond to exceptions and adjustments in the research question, LLM agents can
achieve L2+ level automation. ReseachAgent17 and SciAgent18 show the effectiveness
3


of high-quality research ideas and hypothesis generation with LLM agents. Furthermore,
Coscientist,19 El Agente,20 ChemCrow,21 and MDCrow22 showcase the potential of LLM
agents in accelerating research across diverse domains. Finally, the LangSim project23
shows that LLM agents can perform complex challenges including the design of inverse
materials by mapping desired properties to material conﬁgurations. However, LLM agents
face signiﬁcant challenges in scientiﬁc applications, particularly the ﬁdelity of their results,
their tendency to hallucinate, and their ability to handle complex scientiﬁc challenges:
(i) Most current work is focused on low-ﬁdelity models, leaving high-ﬁdelity calculations
largely unexplored. Density Functional Theory (DFT) is widely used as a high-ﬁdelity
model in materials science, but few LLM agent frameworks incorporate DFT capabilities.
Even when DFT is included, calculation parameters are rarely optimized, potentially lead-
ing to inaccurate results.21,22,24 (ii) LLMs are prone to hallucination, providing false pos-
itive answers or accepting approximately correct results without proper validation. This
decreases result accuracy and is particularly problematic in scientiﬁc applications, where
correctness and reliability are paramount and small errors can cascade into signiﬁcant
inaccuracies. This limitation also prevents the LLM agents from successfully executing
long-horizon or complex tasks.25,26 (iii) Although LLMs provide some level of automation,
their error handling capabilities are typically limited to the tools available to them. Without
carefully designed error-handling protocols, LLM agents can only address trivial errors,
such as ﬁle-not-found exceptions or type errors. Finally, complex convergence errors,
which frequently challenge DFT practitioners, remain beyond the capabilities of existing
frameworks.27,28
Herein, we introduce the DFT-based Research Engine for Agentic Materials Screening
(DREAMS) to address these challenges. As shown in Fig. 1, it is implemented as a hier-
archical, multi-level LLM agent team with dynamic planning capabilities. This architecture
reduces the cognitive load of the LLM and helps mitigate hallucination by distributing tasks
among the specialized LLM agents. These planning capabilities enable complex task han-
4


dling and adaptation to unexpected situations and changing research questions. Further-
more, structure creation tools ensure calculations are performed on physically valid sys-
tems and a shared information dashboard, canvas, maintains key information accessible
to all LLM agents, reducing communication-related hallucinations and enabling complex
multi-step workﬂows. These tools, accessible to all involved LLM agents, are carefully
designed to reduce hallucination and provide guidance on error handling. Finally, a ded-
icated convergence error handling LLM agent further boosts the system’s robustness to
computational challenges encountered in DFT calculations.

To highlight the general applicability of this approach it is tested on three DFT bench-
marks. (1) The capabilities of DREAMS are demonstrated in the Sol27LC dataset29 of
5


bulk material systems, which contains 27 elemental crystals with varying crystal struc-
tures.
Here, DREAMS achieves human expert level accuracy in lattice constant cal-
culation. (2) We challenge DREAMS on the catalyst absorption problem, the famous
“CO/Pt(111) puzzle”.30 It is chosen due to its wide industrial interests31 and yet compu-
tationally difﬁcult and heavily debated30,32,33 due to its sensitivity to calculation settings.
DREAMS manifests human-expert level ability in this puzzle and concludes the same
preference site compared to human experts in the literature.30,33,34 (3) DREAMS analyzes
the uncertainty caused by the choice of exchange-correlation functional using Bayesian
statistics.29 We conﬁrmed the validity of the results calculated by DREAMS by performing
bond length and charge transfer analysis.
The results of our three benchmarks demonstrate that DREAMS can handle high-
level objectives, technical errors and different simulation objectives, approaching L3-level
automation—a signiﬁcant step towards automated materials discovery that accelerates
the identiﬁcation of novel materials for energy storage, catalysis, and other applications.
Results
Problem Statement
The current challenges in applying LLM agents in scientiﬁc re-
search are (1) lack of access to high-ﬁdelity experiments and simulation,21,22,24 (2) su-
perﬁcial error-handling without in-depth analysis due to either lack of tools or limited
reasoning capability,35,36 and (3) the tendency of hallucination and loss of context.37–39
To overcome these challenges, we designed DREAMS: DFT based Research Engine
for Agentic Materials Screening, and the detailed explanation on DREAMS’ architecture
can be found in the Method section. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DREAMS in
scientiﬁc problem-solving by presenting results from three distinct challenges: the lat-
tice constant prediction challenge (Sol27LC benchmark) , the CO adsorption on Pt(111)
surfaces challenge (CO/Pt(111)) and ﬁnally the quantiﬁcation of the uncertainty caused
6


by the choice of exchange-correlation functional. Together, these challenges showcase
DREAMS’s ability to autonomously navigate both routine computational tasks and com-
plex research challenges, i.e., with limited to no human intervention being required.

Exchange Correlation Functional Uncertainty
Upon demonstrating DREAMS’s capability of reproducing human expert level high-ﬁdeltity
DFT simulation results on the CO/Pt(111) puzzle problem, the scope of the challenge was
extended. A natural third challenge from these results is the sensitivity of the adsorption
site preference to the speciﬁc choice of exchange correlation functional at the same level
of theory (GGA). To quantify this uncertainty, DREAMS was asked to perform Bayesian
ensemble sampling with van der Waals correction (BEEF-vdW)29 and the distribution of
possible ∆BEs can be found in Fig. 5 (c). For both human expert’s result and DREAMS’
result, 0 eV, is more than ten standard deviations outside of the distribution of ∆BE, indi-
cating that, even when considering uncertainty, the FCC site remains more energetically
favorable than the ontop site at the GGA level. These results are consistent with our earlier
ﬁndings obtained using the PBE and LDA functionals, as well as with previous literature.30

indicating that fcc adsorption is more favorable at the GGA level.
As for the discrepancies, some possible factors are identiﬁed. First, the convergence
threshold in scf calculations used by DREAMS was higher (1×10−6 Ry) than that used
by the human expert (1×10−7 Ry), despite the lower threshold being recommended in
Quantum ESPRESSO for structure relaxation. Second, although both DREAMS and the
human expert employed the same smearing method, DREAMS set a higher smearing
width of 0.02 Ry compared to the human expert’s setting of 0.01 Ry. This larger smear-
ing width introduces further deviations in the computed adsorption energies. Together,
15


these differences could explain the minor shift observed in DREAMS results relative to
the human expert calculations.
With the adsorbed conﬁgurations explored by DREAMS, we can provide some insight
for the CO/Pt(111) puzzle. We perform Bader charge analysis and bond length analysis,
and the results are shown in Table 5. Recall that DREAMS predicts that FCC site is more
energetically favorable than ontop sites under all three functionals used in this work. We
observe that for all adsorbed CO, the C-O bond length, i.e. dC−O, increases compared
to the pristine CO molecule. The reason for CO bond length increase lies in the electron
transfer from the Pt surface to CO molecule. Upon adsorption, free electrons in Pt metal
partially transfer to C-O bond antibonding Ã∗orbitals, effectively decreasing the bond or-
der of the C-O bond, leading to a bond length increase. In all 3 functionals, the FCC site
probes 0.15-0.18 e−more electron transfer than the ontop site (charge density plots are
available in Supplementary Information S-6), and consequently the C-O bond length is
always longer on the FCC site. The larger degree of electron transfer indicates enhanced
CO-Pt interaction via electron sharing, which explains why CO adsorption is more favored
on the FCC site.34 We would like to point out that the electron transfer from transition metal
surface to CO has actually been studied as early as 1964.43 The mechanism observed in
this work, namely the electron donation from Pt to CO, has been proposed as the back
donation mechanism.34,43 Such a mechanism has been argued to favor FCC site over on-

DREAMS to perform high-ﬁdelity scientiﬁc discovery on general DFT related challenges,
without the need to ﬁne-tune the underlying LLM or the need to provide challenge-speciﬁc
LLM agents.

Discussion
DREAMS showcases the potential of large language model (LLM) agents in address-
ing scientiﬁc challenges in computational materials science. Built upon a hierarchical
multi-agent architecture with structured planning, tool integration, and a shared memory
system, DREAMS is capable of conducting high-ﬁdelity DFT simulations at an automation
level nearing L3, while overcoming key limitations of existing LLM frameworks, such as
hallucination, limited context retention, and insufﬁcient error handling.
The validation of our approach using the Sol27LC benchmark dataset conﬁrms the re-
liability and accuracy of DREAMS for high-ﬁdelity DFT calculations. When applied to the
CO/Pt(111) system, it successfully performed comprehensive adsorption energy calcula-
tions across multiple conﬁgurations, demonstrating the potential of LLM agents to ﬁt in the
high-ﬁdelity material discovery loop. On the exchange-correlation functional uncertainty
benchmark, DREAMS employs Bayesian ensemble sampling with BEEF-vdW to quantify
functional-driven uncertainty, conﬁrming FCC-site preference remains robust across the
ensemble, providing insights into why FCC sites are preferred, and reﬂecting the impact
of DFT parameters on calculation results.
Key innovations in our approach include: (1) carefully designed tools that constrain
the LLM agents behavior without restricting its capabilities, (2) a sophisticated planning
supervisor LLM agent that decomposes complex research challenges into manageable
tasks, (3) a shared canvas structure that supports robust multi-agent communication, and
17


(4) systematic convergence testing procedures that ensure computational accuracy. This
work not only contributes to resolving a speciﬁc puzzle in surface chemistry but also es-
tablishes a generalizable framework for applying LLM agents in computational materials
science and chemistry. Future work could extend this approach to other materials science
challenges and incorporate additional specialized LLM agents with different expertise. We
ﬁnd immense potential of agentic workﬂows in accelerating scientiﬁc discovery by pro-
viding mechanistic insights and identifying overlooked physical factors in computational
modeling, opening new avenues for AI-assisted automated research.
Methods
DREAMS (DFT based Research Engine for Agentic Materials Screening) is implemented
as a hierarchical multi-agent system using the Claude 3.7 Sonnet (20250219)44 API to
provide large language model (LLM) capabilities, constructing a hierarchical agentic work-
ﬂow facilitated by the LangGraph45 framework and applying it to multiple DFT challenges.
For the initial release, the system features three major agents: a planning supervisor LLM
agent and two worker LLM agents, namely a DFT LLM agent and an HPC LLM agent.
Each of the worker LLM agents are built as ReAct Agent46 and incorporate various tools
for execution. These worker LLM agents have reasoning ability to dynamically adapt to
changing task requirements as well as handle exceptions, while actions allow them to
interface with built-in functions as tools. Their system prompts are formatted into four sec-
tions: ïRoleð, ïObjectiveð, ïInstructionð, and ïRequirementð. An example is provided in
the Supplementary Information S-7 to S-8. Based on a given prompt, these LLM agents
can complete speciﬁc tasks by using the tools available to them. DREAMS’s tools are
designed to balance scientiﬁc ﬂexibility with deterministic behavior, minimizing opportuni-
ties for hallucinated outputs. Unlike traditional hard-coded functions or workﬂows, each of
DREAMS tools is implemented as an agentic tool with a built-in LLM interface, enabling
18


contextual understanding while enforcing strict scientiﬁc constraints. The LLM tools in-
corporate rigorous validation checks and produce informative error messages to facilitate
LLM agent self-correction. Finally, a canvas is provided and shared among all worker
LLM agents, tools, and users to mitigate the hallucination challenge. This hierarchical
approach was chosen for its ﬂexibility and ability to manage complex interactions among
multiple LLM agents, as well as its extendability.
Dynamic Planning
The planning LLM supervisor agent plays a central role in orchestrating the overall work-
ﬂow.
Unlike simple task schedulers, the supervisor LLM agent decomposes complex
research objectives into manageable subtasks tailored to each worker LLM agent’s ca-
pabilities. It operates on a dictionary containing ﬁve ﬁelds: input, plan, past steps,
response, and next. The input ﬁeld stores the user-provided objective. The plan holds
the current plan of actions. The past steps ﬁeld records summaries of completed steps.
The response contains the ﬁnal answer generated by the planning supervisor LLM agent,
and next speciﬁes the next LLM agent to be called. At the beginning, only the input ﬁeld
is populated with the user’s objective. The planning supervisor LLM agent then breaks
down the objective into smaller, well-deﬁned tasks based on the capabilities and con-
straints of available worker LLM agents. It writes these tasks into the plan, selects the
next LLM agent to act, and updates the next ﬁeld accordingly. Once a worker LLM agent
completes a task, its response is summarized and recorded in the past steps ﬁeld. The
planning supervisor LLM agent then revises the plan based on three components: (1) the
original research objective, (2) the current state of the plan, and (3) the history of com-
pleted steps. This process is repeated iteratively. Once the objective is fully addressed,
the supervisor LLM agent writes the ﬁnal result to the response ﬁeld, terminates the work-
ﬂow, and returns the result to the user. This hierarchical planning strategy reduces the
cognitive load on individual LLM agents and mitigates context window overﬂow by nar-
19


rowing the active context to only the relevant task history. As a result, LLM agents are
less likely to hallucinate during long-running workﬂows, and the example of which can be
found under the result section.
DFT LLM Agent
The DFT LLM Agent functions as a specialized worker LLM agent with computational
chemistry expertise focused on high-ﬁdelity density functional theory (DFT) calculations.
This LLM agent is responsible for managing the scientiﬁc aspects of electronic structure
calculations, including the construction of atomistic models, optimization of computational
parameters, and analysis of calculation results. The DFT LLM agent’s core functions in-
clude: (1) generating atomistic structures such as bulk crystals, surfaces, and adsorbate
conﬁgurations; (2) determining suitable DFT convergence parameters through systematic
convergence testing; (3) preparing input ﬁles for quantum chemistry software; and (4) an-
alyzing outputs and extract physical properties, including lattice constants and adsorption
energies. To perform these tasks, the DFT LLM agent is equipped with a suite of tools,
each designed for a speciﬁc purpose. The LLM agent selects tools based on their doc-
umented capabilities. Further details of these tools are provided in the Supplementary
Information S-12 to S-18.
The tools of the DFT LLM agent are interfaced through established frameworks such
as the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE),47 preventing unsafe operations like direct
ﬁle manipulation, which can otherwise lead to invalid structures or runtime failures. Each
tool maintains explicit input-output mappings and implements comprehensive error han-
dling. For example, the adsorption energy tool requires exactly three DFT output ﬁles
(clean slab, isolated adsorbate, and adsorbate-on-slab) and applies standard thermody-
namic formulas to compute results. This architecture prevents the use of hallucinated
parameters or unphysical equations, ensuring scientiﬁc correctness. To further reduce
complexity and redundancy, we developed a batch modiﬁcation tool for convergence test-
20


ing, enabling the rapid generation of Quantum ESPRESSO (QE)48 scripts based on a
template. This optimization reduces the complexity of script generation from O(N) to O(1)
by modifying only the speciﬁed convergence parameters while preserving the remainder
of the input, signiﬁcantly lowering the risk of inconsistencies or human error.
Atomistic Structure Generation
In the benchmarking experiment on the CO/Pt(111) system, we utilize the AutoCat li-
brary15 as a computational framework for generating and analyzing adsorption structures.
Compared to simply letting the LLM decide the atomistic structures, using AutoCat to con-
trol the structural degrees of freedom ensures that the structures to be simulated are phys-
ically meaningful. For example, DREAMS can create structures with different adsorbate
sites, surface slab sizes, vacuum spacing, adsorbate orientations, coverage patterns, and
adsorption heights, and we are conﬁdent that the structures are physically meaningful, as
illustrated in Fig. 5 (a).
Implementing domain knowledge through AutoCat also avoids redundant conﬁgura-
tions. For example, for Pt with FCC crystal structure, the (111) surface has only 4 distinct
adsorption sites, namely the ontop, bridge, FCC and HCP sites. However, if such symme-
try constraints are not known in advance, a grid-search with a 0.1Å spacing would result
in 121 possible adsorption sites, which is almost 30 times the computation cost.
In conclusion, AutoCat abstracts these low-level conﬁgurational operations behind a
structured API, allowing LLM agents to invoke high-level actions such as “generate FCC
adsorption structures with all relevant CO orientations” without having to reason about
individual atomic coordinates or manually deﬁne geometry constraints. The integration of
such carefully designed tool thus enables reliable and efﬁcient exploration of a chemically
rich conﬁguration space that would otherwise be prone to failure or hallucination if handled
entirely at the LLM level.
21


Convergence LLM Agent
The convergence LLM agent is implemented as a large language model (LLM) embedded
within a tool. To use this tool, the DFT LLM agent must ﬁrst specify which job has encoun-
tered a convergence issue. The tool then locates the relevant ﬁles for that job and, for
each ﬁle, prompts the LLM with the following query: Here is the content of the file
<content>, please give me suggestions on how to fix the convergence issue. The
LLM is instructed to provide a structured and concise response to the formatted question.
In this setup, most operational tasks, such as parameter parsing and preprocessing, are
handled deterministically by code. This allows the LLM to focus exclusively on decision-
making. Additionally, by decoupling the LLM from the broader LLM agent communication
graph, the LLM agent can concentrate on context-speciﬁc questions without the complex-
ity of managing inter-agent interactions. This design enhances both the robustness and
success rate of convergence handling. The convergence LLM agent is able to provide
suggestions in parameter setting and script generation, and the reasoning process, and
enables the DFT LLM agent to self-correct and conduct updated calculations. Represen-
tative suggestions are shown in Table 3.
HPC LLM Agent
The HPC LLM Agent acts as a specialized High-Performance Computing (HPC) resource
manager. Its core responsibilities include: (1) optimizing computational resource alloca-
tion based on the complexity of the calculation; (2) scheduling and submitting DFT calcu-
lations to appropriate HPC clusters; (3) monitoring calculation status and progress; and
(4) retrieving and organizing output ﬁles upon completion. To ensure efﬁcient resource us-
age, the HPC LLM agent dynamically selects computational parameters—such as node
count, processor allocation, partition, and walltime—based on calculation-speciﬁc infor-
mation, including system size, calculation type, and settings.
22


The LLM agent is equipped with a suite of tools designed to support these tasks. It
selects tools based on their documented capabilities. Further details of these tools are
provided in the Supplementary Information S-12 to S-18. For calculation submission, the
LLM agent employs the Python Simple Queuing System Adapter (pysqa),13 which pro-
vides seamless integration with SLURM-based49 HPC environments. This abstraction
layer decouples the scientiﬁc logic from infrastructure-speciﬁc details, enabling the frame-
work to remain focused on computational chemistry tasks while making effective use of
available computational resources.
Canvas
Canvas is a shared information dashboard that enables lossless and time-invariant data
sharing among LLM agents, tools, and human users. It stores all variables in their native
format, reducing errors and preventing hallucinations that may arise from converting data
to and from text. Before executing any task, LLM agents inspect the canvas to retrieve rel-
evant information and record important results back into canvas when appropriate. Fig. 6
shows an example snapshot from a CO/Pt(111) workﬂow. In this example, when the LLM
agent encounters a convergence issue for the second time, it ﬁrst reviews the previous pa-
rameter settings stored under convergence_modifications. It then uses this information
to request updated DFT setting suggestions. Next, it retrieves the corresponding struc-
ture ﬁle from Pt111_CO_upright_path, veriﬁes and loads the correct pseudopotentials
from canvas, and ﬁnally generates a new set of calculations, avoid repetitively generat-
ing structures and searching pseudopotentials. This process demonstrates how canvas
helps maintain data consistency in long-running workﬂows and prevents redundant oper-
ations. Full snapshot of canvas from Sol27LC and CO/Pt(111) challenge can be found in
Supplementary Information S-2 and Supplementary Information S-9 to S-11.
All information in the canvas are stored in a centralized dictionary object. In addi-
tion, the canvas provides several functions to support core operations. The three main

DFT Benchmark
Density functional theory (DFT) is one of the most widely employed ﬁrst-principles simu-
lation methods for atomistic systems. A number of softwares packages have been devel-
oped to carry out these calculations, including VASP,50 Gaussian,51 Quantum Espresso
(QE),48 etc.
In this work, we use QE v7.2 for DFT calculations, which uses the plane wave (PW) ba-
sis set for describing electron wavefunctions, and uses pseudopotentials (PP) to describe
core electrons. We also investigate the impact of exchange correlation functional (XC)
choices on calculated structural properties, including the lattice constant and adsorption
energies. These include functionals under the Local Density Approximation (LDA) and
the generalized gradient approximation (GGA), namely Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE)
functional and the PW91 functional. All the calculations are carried out using the GBRV
pseudopotentials.
The lattice constant values are obtained from ﬁtting an equation of state (EOS) curve
25


between DFT-calculated potential energy and volume, and ﬁnding the lowest-energy point.
These values are benchmarked using the Sol27LC dataset, which was collected in Ref.29
and includes lattice constants of 27 elemental crystals in BCC, FCC, and diamond lat-
tices. The elements in this dataset covers both metals and non-metals, which makes it
ideal for testing DREMAS’ ability across the periodic table. The adsorption energies are
calculated as:
Eads = ECO−Pt(111) −ECO −EPt(111)

where ECO−Pt(111), ECO and EPt(111) are the potential energies of the Pt(111) slab with a
CO molecule adsorbed on top, the single CO molecule, and the clean Pt(111) surface,
correspondingly. The results in this work are benchmarked against results produced by
Peter et. al, 30 who systematically analyzed CO adsorption on Pt(111) using a range
of DFT implementations and settings. For uncertainty quantiﬁcation, the Bayesian error
estimation functional with van der Waals correction (BEEF-vdW) is used. We use a total
of 2,000 functionals in our ensemble to sample the energy distribution.52
